claims.text: The equimolar WTaTiVZr alloy has improved plastic strain relative to pure tungsten at high temperature.
The equimolar WTaTiVZr alloy has improved toughness relative to pure tungsten at high temperature.
Enhanced lattice distortion caused by adding Ta, Ti, V, and Zr contributes to the alloy's improved plastic strain and toughness.
Nanoscale precipitate formation from the added refractory elements contributes to the alloy's improved plastic strain and toughness.
The proposed microstructural complexity disrupts conventional dislocation glide relative to tungsten.
Disruption of dislocation glide produces more effective work hardening.
The proposed microstructural complexity delays crack propagation during high-temperature loading.
The initial WTaTiVZr alloy is homogeneous and equimolar.
The initial WTaTiVZr alloy has a fine-grained microstructure.
Commercially used pure tungsten has a relatively coarse and brittle microstructure.
Ta, Ti, V, and Zr additions drive formation of nanoscale precipitates or secondary phases.
Nanoscale precipitates or secondary phases act as obstacles to dislocation movement.
Lattice distortion and nanoscale precipitates promote more diffuse plastic deformation in WTaTiVZr.
Under equivalent high-temperature loading, WTaTiVZr will exhibit greater work hardening than pure tungsten.
Under equivalent high-temperature loading, WTaTiVZr will exhibit greater fracture toughness than pure tungsten.
Post-test analysis of WTaTiVZr will reveal nanoscale precipitates and altered dislocation structures.
Pure tungsten typically has limited plasticity and lower fracture toughness under high-temperature mechanical loading.
Pure tungsten's proposed brittle failure results from easier and more catastrophic dislocation movement.
The proposed mechanism applies primarily at temperatures where thermal activation permits evolution of precipitates and dislocation structures.
At lower temperatures, the performance difference may decrease because diffusion and precipitate formation become limited.
